title: The Smallest Shader
objective: Separate placing vertices from coloring fragments.

terms.Vertex: A mesh point processed before rasterization
terms.Fragment: A candidate sample produced by rasterization
terms.Uniform: A material parameter shared by shader invocations

exercise: Make an unshaded Godot material with a color uniform. Change the color, then rotate the mesh. Explain which change alters the flat color and why.
checks: Rotation changes the silhouette, not the chosen color.
The material exposes its color in the Inspector.
recap: The vertex stage positions the mesh.
The fragment stage supplies its color.
A uniform exposes a material control.
Unshaded output has no built-in lighting.
beats: This shader has two jobs. The vertex function places mesh points. Rasterization turns triangles into fragments. The fragment function assigns their color. Neither function needs to know the whole picture.
Read the matrix chain from right to left. Model places the object in the world. View expresses that world relative to the camera. Projection produces clip coordinates.
The fourth coordinate is one because this is a position. Translation must affect it. The result is a four-component clip position; perspective division comes later in the rendering pipeline.
Now the fragment function writes the same uniform color everywhere. The sphere loses its shading cues and looks like a flat disc. Its geometry has not disappeared.
Watch the color change from teal to terracotta. Every visible fragment receives the new material value. We changed an input, not the triangle mesh or the shader program.
Unshaded means Godot does not add its built-in lighting here. A light node will not create a highlight on this material. The silhouette still comes from the mesh.
The source-color hint identifies a color input. In Forward Plus, color conversion matters. A displayed color is not automatically the same numeric quantity as a linear-light shader value.

Writing POSITION makes this shader responsible for the entire clip position. Godot can normally do that transformation for you. Keep this explicit version to understand the pipeline, not because every material requires it.

title: Passing Normals to Pixels
objective: Trace a surface normal from the mesh through a varying into fragment lighting.
wrong: the normal is already in world space
right: the normal needs a space conversion

terms.Normal: A direction perpendicular to the surface
terms.World space: Coordinates shared by objects and lights
terms.Varying: A value passed and interpolated between shader stages

exercise: Rotate a Godot mesh using this shader. Trace its normal through the vertex function, varying, and fragment function. Explain why the light direction and normal must use the same coordinate space.
checks: The normal is transformed before the dot product.
The interpolated normal is normalized again.
recap: Mesh normals start in local space.
The normal matrix carries them to world space.
Varyings interpolate across triangles.
Normalize before comparing directions.
beats: The input normal belongs to the mesh's local coordinates. Our light direction is defined in world coordinates. Comparing them directly would compare directions expressed in different reference frames.
The vertex function multiplies the normal by the model normal matrix. This is a direction transformation, not a position transformation. Translation must not move a normal.
The varying carries transformed normals toward the fragment stage. Rasterization interpolates their components across each triangle. It does not run the vertex function again for every fragment.
Interpolation can change a vector's length. Normalize the interpolated normal before using it in a dot product. Otherwise its length would accidentally change the brightness.
Watch the torus rotate while the light remains fixed in world space. Different surface directions face the light. The normal transformation is what keeps those directions consistent with the scene.
This uniform stores the direction light travels. Lighting needs the direction toward the light. The minus sign converts between those conventions; removing it illuminates the opposite side.
The normalized directions meet in a clamped dot product. A surface facing the light gets a positive weight. A surface facing away gets zero. That weight multiplies the surface color.
Despite its name, the base shader already implements Lambert lighting. Its executable code matches the separate Lambert file. This lesson is about the data path, not a new lighting model.

title: Lambert: Light Is an Angle
objective: Predict diffuse brightness from the dot product of normalized directions.

terms.Dot product: A measure of alignment between directions
terms.Clamp: Restrict a value to a specified interval

exercise: For unit directions separated by zero, sixty, and ninety degrees, predict the Lambert weights. Then rotate the light in Godot and explain why the back-facing side stays black.
checks: The predicted weights are one, one half, and zero.
Negative dot products are clamped to zero.
recap: Normalize both directions.
Their dot product measures alignment.
Clamp away negative light.
This directional-light model has no distance attenuation.
beats: Start with a unit surface normal and a unit direction toward the light. Their dot product is the cosine of the angle between them. That is the entire diffuse brightness model here.
When both directions line up, the dot product is one. Multiply the surface color by one and its diffuse contribution reaches full strength. This is a lighting weight, not a screen-byte measurement.
At sixty degrees, the dot product is one half. The diffuse contribution is halved before display conversion. Do not assume the displayed pixel will be half as bright numerically.
At ninety degrees, the dot product reaches zero. Beyond ninety degrees it becomes negative. Clamp removes that negative contribution; the back of the object cannot receive negative light.
Watch the direction rotate around the object. The bright region follows the surfaces facing the incoming light. We never changed a light's distance, because this shader has no light position.
The stored direction points along the traveling light. Negating it points back toward the source. If the vector points upward before negation, the shader lights downward-facing surfaces.
The normal is transformed into world space before interpolation. The light direction is also world space. A plausible-looking dot product can still be wrong when its vectors use different spaces.

This manually computed Lambert material does not ask Godot for scene-light shadows or distance falloff. It teaches one mechanism: surface orientation controls the diffuse term. Those other effects need additional machinery.

title: Ambient: The Lighting Floor
objective: Distinguish a constant ambient approximation from simulated bounced light.
exercise: Set ambient color to black, then raise it gradually. Predict which side of the object changes most visibly. Explain why this constant term cannot reproduce contact shadows.
checks: The previously dark side becomes visible.
No geometry-dependent occlusion is computed.
recap: Ambient is added to the diffuse weight.
The surface color multiplies both contributions.
A constant floor cannot compute occlusion.
Color conversion changes the arithmetic values.
beats: Lambert alone returns zero on the back-facing side. Real scenes often contain indirect illumination. This shader uses a constant ambient color as a cheap stand-in for that missing light.
Look at the parentheses. Ambient is added to the Lambert term first. The sum is multiplied by the surface color, so the background contribution inherits the same surface tint.
Start with ambient set to black. That adds nothing. The material returns to plain Lambert behavior, which gives us a clean baseline for seeing what the extra term does.
Now raise ambient gradually. The dark side becomes visible even where the light-facing dot product is zero. This reveals color; it does not calculate the shape of bounced illumination.
A Color Is Not A Weight
The ambient input is marked as a color. In Forward Plus, an sRGB gray of zero point fifteen converts to roughly zero point zero one nine six in linear light.

That conversion means the Forward Plus sum is not automatically one plus zero point fifteen. Add the values the shader actually receives. Display colors and linear-light contributions are different quantities.
There is no neighborhood query in this shader. An exposed surface and a hidden crevice receive the same ambient input. A constant floor cannot produce contact shadows or color bleeding.

Use this material to separate the direct-light term from an ambient approximation. If you need convincing indirect illumination, this constant alone is insufficient. The useful lesson is where each contribution enters.

title: Fresnel: The View-Dependent Rim
objective: Explain the artistic rim weight and distinguish it from physical Fresnel reflectance.
wrong: the rim depends only on the lamp
right: the rim also depends on the viewer

terms.Eye vector: Direction from the surface toward the camera
terms.Silhouette: The visible outline of an object
terms.Exponent: A power controlling the rim's concentration

exercise: Compare Fresnel powers of one, three, and six. Predict whether the bright rim gets wider or narrower. Explain why this shader's rim can still fade on the unlit side.
checks: Larger positive powers narrow the rim.
The rim is multiplied by the lighting term.
recap: The view-normal angle drives the rim.
A higher positive exponent narrows it.
Lighting modulates the rim in this shader.
This is an artistic approximation to Fresnel behavior.
beats: Diffuse shading uses the light direction. A rim needs another direction: from the surface toward the camera. The vertex function computes that vector in world space and passes it onward.
Normalize the eye vector and compare it with the normal. When they align, their dot product is one. Subtracting that from one makes the rim weight zero.
Toward the silhouette, the view and normal become nearly perpendicular. Their dot product approaches zero, so the rim's base approaches one. That is why the effect gathers at the edge.
For a base between zero and one, a larger positive exponent reduces intermediate values. Watch the power increase: the transition tightens toward the silhouette. The rim becomes narrower.
If the view-normal dot product is one half, the base is also one half. Cubing it gives one eighth. That is the geometric rim weight before the lighting factor multiplies it.

This implementation multiplies the rim by Lambert plus ambient. The dark side therefore receives a smaller rim contribution. An angle-based effect does not automatically glow independently of lighting.
The shader adds the rim to the base color. It does not conserve reflected energy or calculate a material's refractive index. Call this a Fresnel-inspired rim, not complete physical reflectance.
Camera position comes from the inverse view matrix's translation column. Move the camera and the rim follows the new view direction. Its behavior belongs to the surface-camera relationship.

title: Phong: The Moving Highlight
objective: Explain why a specular highlight depends on view direction and exponent.
right: the highlight is computed from directions

terms.Reflection: Mirroring a direction around the surface normal

exercise: Compare specular powers of eight and one hundred while keeping the light fixed. Then move the camera. Explain the highlight's width and why it is not attached like painted texture.
checks: Higher power produces a tighter highlight.
Camera movement changes the highlight position.
recap: Reflect the view direction about the normal.
Compare that reflected direction with the light.
The exponent controls the highlight's width.
This Phong model is an artistic lighting approximation.
beats: A painted white spot stays attached to the object. A reflection highlight depends on where the viewer stands. This shader introduces the eye vector alongside the surface normal and light direction.
The eye vector points away from the surface. The shader negates its reflected value to obtain the outward mirror direction. The sign matters because reflect expects an incident direction.
The mirrored direction is compared with the direction toward the light. Alignment produces a value near one. Misalignment reduces it. Clamp prevents negative values from entering the power.
Raise that alignment to a positive power. A larger exponent suppresses everything except close alignment. Watch the highlight tighten as the power increases from eight toward one hundred.
The highlight has its own color control. Its contribution is added after the diffuse term. That is why changing the base color does not simply repaint every highlight by the same factor.

The final line combines diffuse lighting, ambient, the rim, and this highlight. Reading those terms separately lets you identify which control changes a broad shading gradient and which changes the bright spot.
This is a manually specified directional light. The shader does not trace a ray to a lamp or ask whether another object blocks it. A highlight is not proof of a traced reflection.

Phong gives a compact model for a shiny lobe. The exponent is an artistic concentration control, not a physical roughness measurement. The key mechanism is the relationship among light, normal, and viewer.

title: Diffuse Maps: Paint Before Light
objective: Trace a color texture through UV sampling and diffuse multiplication.
right: the texture colors the diffuse term

terms.UV: Two-dimensional coordinates used to address a texture
terms.Sampler: A shader input used to read texture data

exercise: Change shader color while keeping the checker texture and lighting fixed. Predict which contribution is tinted. Explain why the additive highlight does not follow the same multiplication.
checks: The base texture is multiplied by shader color.
The highlight is added after the diffuse multiplication.
recap: UV coordinates select the texture sample.
Color textures use the source-color hint.
The sampled color multiplies the diffuse base.
Rim and highlight are added separately.
beats: The shader reads a two-dimensional texture at the mesh's UV coordinates. Those coordinates address the picture. They are not world positions, and they do not add geometry to the sphere.
The sampler declares a color texture with the source-color hint. This identifies the stored color encoding so Forward Plus can use appropriate values for lighting arithmetic.
The texture's red, green, and blue channels multiply shader color. White tint preserves the texture. A colored tint changes the base without changing which texels the UV coordinates select.
The tinted texture is multiplied by Lambert plus ambient. A checker cell still becomes dark when its surface faces away from the light. The texture does not replace the lighting calculation.
Watch the tint move from white toward terracotta. The checker colors change together because they share the same material uniform. Their positions on the mesh remain fixed.
The rim and specular highlight are added afterward. They are not multiplied by the diffuse texture in this implementation. That separation is visible where a bright highlight crosses painted cells.

The repeat hint explicitly requests tiling outside the usual UV interval. State that intent instead of relying on an assumed sampler default. UV transforms later make this choice particularly visible.

A diffuse map changes color, not normals or silhouette. To distinguish these effects, keep the mesh and light fixed while changing only the color map. The shader's data path tells you what can change.

title: Specular Maps: Where It Shines
objective: Explain independently packed masks for rim and highlight strength.

terms.Mask: A number controlling a contribution's strength
terms.Channel: One component of a texture sample

exercise: Paint the red and green channels of the specular map separately. Predict which channel changes the rim and which changes the highlight. Test a zero mask and a one mask.
checks: Red masks the rim; green masks the highlight.
Mask values are read without source-color conversion.
recap: The specular texture carries data masks.
Red controls this shader's rim strength.
Green controls its highlight strength.
This rim no longer has the diffuse lighting factor.
beats: A texture sample can hold controls rather than paint. Here the red channel is a rim mask and the green channel is a highlight mask. Blue does not contribute to either term.
Multiply the rim contribution by red. A zero removes it at that texel. A one preserves it. Intermediate values scale the contribution, allowing a patterned rim on one material.
Green independently scales the Phong highlight. A matte cell can suppress a highlight even when the reflection directions line up. Its neighboring cell can retain the same lighting lobe.
The mask sampler has no source-color hint. These values are controls, not display colors. Color conversion would change intermediate mask strengths and therefore change the material's response.
Compare an all-white mask with the packed texture. First both effects are allowed everywhere. Then patterned regions suppress them independently. The geometry and light stay the same.
There is another change in this file: the rim is no longer multiplied by Lambert plus ambient. The mask addition is not the only difference from the diffuse-map shader.
Because that lighting factor is absent, the rim can remain bright on the unlit side. Do not diagnose that glow as a broken specular map. It follows directly from the changed rim formula.
Channel meanings belong to this shader. Another material might use red for a different purpose. Read the channel contract before reusing the texture; a valid image can still drive the wrong effect.

title: Normal Maps Without New Geometry
objective: Explain tangent-space normal decoding and its unchanged silhouette.

terms.Binormal: The second direction along the surface
terms.Tangent space: Coordinates relative to the local surface frame

exercise: Compare a flat normal map with the dome map. Inspect the outline, then invert green. Explain why the lighting changes while the mesh silhouette remains the same.
checks: The silhouette stays unchanged.
The green convention matches the expected map.
recap: Decode the texture into signed components.
Use the tangent frame to obtain a world normal.
Lighting uses the perturbed direction.
The mesh silhouette remains unchanged.
beats: The normal map stores direction components in RGB. Multiplying by two and subtracting one converts the stored zero-to-one range into signed components between minus one and one.
Tangent, binormal, and normal form the surface frame. The vertex stage carries these directions into world space so the sampled direction can be expressed where the light and eye vectors live.
The sampled red component weights the tangent, green weights the binormal, and blue weights the normal. Add the weighted directions and normalize the result. That becomes the lighting normal.
The perturbed normal drives diffuse, rim, and specular calculations. The shader does not merely paint shadows onto the texture. It changes the direction used by the lighting formulas.
Compare a flat map with the dome map. The surface appears bumpy because the directions vary across each cell. Look at the outside edge: the actual sphere has not grown those domes.
This version expects the supplied OpenGL-style map. A DirectX-style green channel has the opposite sign. Flipping that channel without adapting the shader reverses the vertical lighting detail.

This teaching port transforms tangents with the normal matrix too. That agrees for uniform scale, but it is not a general tangent-frame solution for nonuniform scaling. Keep this demonstration uniformly scaled.
All the apparent bumps happen in the fragment lighting. There is no vertex displacement here. If the outline must change, a normal map alone cannot provide that geometry.

title: Cube Maps: A Stored World
objective: Explain direction-based environment lookup and rim weighting.
right: the reflection samples a stored world

terms.Cubemap: Six images addressed by a direction
terms.Reflection vector: The direction used to look into the environment
terms.Rim weight: A view-dependent multiplier near the silhouette

exercise: Move the camera while keeping the cubemap fixed. Then add an unrelated object to the scene. Explain which change affects the lookup and why the new object does not appear automatically.
checks: The reflection direction changes with the camera.
A static cubemap does not capture new scene objects.
recap: A direction selects a cubemap sample.
The reflection vector depends on the viewer.
The rim weights the reflection in this shader.
The cubemap is not a live scene reflection.
beats: A cubemap stores surroundings on six faces. The shader addresses it with a three-dimensional direction, not the mesh's two-dimensional UV coordinates. The runtime assembles the six generated test images.
Normalize the eye vector and normal, then mirror the eye direction with the correct sign. This produces the direction into the stored environment that should appear at this surface point.
The texture call reads the cubemap along that reflection direction. It does not trace through the current scene. The returned color is whatever the stored environment contains there.
The environment sample is multiplied by the rim term before being added. That term depends on both the viewing angle and the diffuse-plus-ambient lighting factor in this implementation.
Watch the camera move while the environment stays fixed. The eye vectors change, so the lookup directions change. The reflected pattern can move without replacing any cubemap image.

At a point facing directly toward the camera, the rim's geometric weight is zero. Its cubemap contribution disappears there. That missing reflection is a consequence of the formula, not a failed texture.
The Phong highlight remains a separate addition. A bright center does not prove the cubemap is contributing at that point. Separate the highlight and environment terms when debugging.

Adding a moving object beside this sphere will not put that object into the stored cubemap. For dynamic local reflections, you need additional rendering machinery. This shader teaches the lookup and its weighting.

title: Vertex Animation: Moving the Mesh
objective: Trace a time-dependent displacement and recognize stale lighting inputs.
right: deformation also needs updated lighting inputs

terms.Vertex: A mesh position processed by the vertex stage
terms.Amplitude: The size and direction of an offset
terms.Frequency: How quickly a phase varies across space

exercise: Set the vertex offset to zero, then raise its vertical component. Compare silhouette motion with the highlight. Explain which lighting inputs would need updating for a physically consistent deformed surface.
checks: Zero offset produces no displacement.
The current shader retains its original normal and eye vector.
recap: A sine wave controls the displacement.
Time animates its phase.
The offset sets amplitude and direction.
The port retains undeformed lighting inputs.
beats: The vertex function adds an offset to the mesh position before Godot projects it. Unlike normal mapping, this operation really moves mesh vertices and can change the visible outline.
The sine receives time multiplied by speed, plus the original horizontal position multiplied by frequency. Time moves the wave forward. Position makes different vertices sit at different phases.
The offset vector controls both amplitude and direction. A vertical offset makes an up-and-down deformation. A sideways offset pushes along a different local axis. It is an object-space displacement.
If the offset is zero, multiplying it by any sine value still produces zero. The untouched default shader does not wobble. The demo material supplies a nonzero override to make the effect visible.
Watch the vertical offset grow. The silhouette now moves because actual vertices move. The finite mesh resolution limits how smoothly that displacement can describe the intended wave.
Before changing VERTEX, this port computes the world position used for the eye vector. It therefore keeps the direction to the original position, not the displaced one.
The normal is also carried from the original mesh. It is not recomputed from the deformed surface. A moving outline with inconsistent shading is an expected limitation of this teaching port.

For a more complete deformation, update the lighting position and derive suitable deformed normals. The lesson here is the vertex displacement mechanism and the extra responsibilities that come with moving geometry.

title: UV Manipulation: Moving the Address
objective: Explain centered tiling, translation, and time-based UV scrolling.
right: larger UV scale repeats more tiles

terms.UV: The address used to sample a texture
terms.Translation: An offset added to the sampling address

exercise: Set UV scale to one, then two, with translation and scrolling disabled. Predict the number of repeats. Then enable scrolling and explain why the object itself does not move.
checks: Scale two produces more repetitions.
Diffuse, mask, and normal reads share the transformed UV.
recap: Subtract one half to center the transform.
Scale and translate the sampling address.
Time adds a scrolling offset.
All three maps use the same transformed UV.
beats: This shader changes the coordinates passed to its texture reads. It does not move the mesh. The same surface fragments now ask for different locations in the stored images.
Subtract one half before scaling and add it back afterward. That makes the center of the UV square the pivot for the scale, instead of the corner.
A scale of two makes the UV coordinates cover twice the interval along each axis. With repeating enabled, more copies fit across the surface. The apparent texture features become smaller.

The translation components add a fixed offset. Time multiplied by speed adds a changing offset. These are sampling movements; the visible pattern can travel opposite the direction you move the address.
In the capture, scale increases while a small horizontal scrolling speed remains active. The tiles become smaller and slide. The sphere and torus keep their geometry and positions.
The transformed coordinates feed the normal map as well as the color and specular maps. Using the original UV for just one would make the lighting detail slip out of alignment with the paint.

Set scale to one, translation to zero, and speed to zero. The expression returns the original UV coordinates. That identity case gives a direct check against the normal-mapped material without the transform.

The texture addresses move, but the tangent frame stays attached to the mesh. This positive-scale, scrolling demonstration works within that limitation. Mirroring or rotating normal-map coordinates needs extra attention to direction conventions.

title: Render States: Four Behaviors
objective: Distinguish shading calculations from opaque, blended, cutout, and additive rendering.
right: render state determines how alpha is used

terms.Blend: Combine a fragment with the background
terms.Cutout: Discard fragments below an alpha threshold

exercise: Compare opaque, alpha blend, alpha scissor, and additive modes using the same rim alpha. Explain whether each pixel replaces, mixes with, disappears from, or brightens the background.
checks: Cutout discards instead of partially mixing.
Additive brightens the destination rather than replacing it.
recap: The shading formula and render state are separate.
Opaque output ignores the unused rim alpha.
Blending mixes; scissor discards.
Additive contributes light to the background.
beats: This file keeps the lighting calculation largely shared and selects a rendering behavior with a compile-time definition. The number chooses the render mode; it is not a runtime material slider.
In opaque mode, the shader does not write ALPHA. The rim can still affect color, but it does not make the object transparent. Alpha's existence in another branch does not change this selected branch.
The blending mode writes the rim value to alpha. Small alpha reveals more background; larger alpha contributes more object color. In this model, the front-facing center can become nearly transparent.
Alpha scissor uses a threshold of zero point three. Values below that threshold are discarded. This is a cutout decision, not a partially transparent mixture with the background.

Watch the same material cycle through opaque, blended, scissored, and additive variants. The geometry and lighting formula stay shared. The different silhouettes and background interactions come from rendering state.
Additive rendering contributes the fragment's color weighted by alpha to the destination. It can brighten the background. It does not behave like an opaque coat of paint.

The original lesson discarded values equal to the threshold too. This Godot alpha-scissor version keeps the equality boundary. That tiny difference is documented rather than claimed as a bit-exact port.
These are four alternatives, not four passes stacked together. Choose one compiled variant for a material. A multi-pass effect is a different design, and this file does not implement one.

title: Blend Maps: Three Colors
objective: Read channel-weighted color mixing without assuming RGB naming order.
wrong: the channels follow the color names
right: the code defines the channel mapping

terms.Weight: A multiplier applied to a contribution
terms.Blend map: A texture whose components choose mixture weights

exercise: Set the first color to yellow, the second to cyan, and the third to magenta. Predict the output in pure red, blue, and green regions of the blend map. Then inspect the shader's channel order.
checks: Red selects the first color; blue selects the second.
Green selects the third color.
recap: Texture channels supply mixture weights.
The order here is red, blue, then green.
Weights are not normalized by this shader.
Lighting is applied after choosing the base color.
beats: The blend texture stores weights. Its channels do not have to be the final visible colors. The material supplies three separate colors that those weights will combine.
Read the expression carefully. Red weights shader color. Blue weights blended color. Green weights third color. The second and third names do not follow the usual red, green, blue reading order.
A pure red texel has a red weight of one and the other weights zero. Only the first color survives. Pure blue selects the second; pure green selects the third.
Intermediate channel values create mixtures. This expression simply adds weighted colors. It does not divide by the sum of weights, so arbitrary maps can make the mixture brighter or darker.
Watch the first material color change from red toward yellow. Only regions controlled by the blend map's red channel respond directly. The blue and green selections retain their own colors.

The combined base color is multiplied by diffuse plus ambient lighting. Rim and highlight are added separately. Color selection and surface illumination remain distinguishable parts of the calculation.

The blend sampler is not marked source color because its channels are weights. Treating those intermediate numbers as display colors would change the mixture. The three actual paint uniforms are marked as colors.

When a region changes the wrong paint, inspect the channel mapping before repainting the texture. The shader is authoritative: texture names and familiar RGB ordering cannot tell you the mapping by themselves.

title: Car Paint: Tuning Reflections
objective: Separate reflection controls from the two specular highlight lobes.
wrong: car paint is one shine control

terms.Reflection floor: An added baseline in the rim weight
terms.Contrast power: An exponent applied to cubemap color

exercise: Raise Fresnel offset while keeping intensity fixed, then compare the two specular powers. Explain which change adds front-facing reflection and which changes highlight width.
checks: Offset allows a nonzero front-facing reflection weight.
The two powers shape separate highlight contributions.
recap: Intensity scales the angle-based reflection term.
Offset adds a reflection baseline before lighting.
A power reshapes the cubemap color.
Two specular lobes contribute separate highlights.
beats: This shader extends a rim-weighted environment lookup. Intensity scales the angular part, while offset adds a baseline. The two controls are not interchangeable even when both make some regions brighter.

With zero offset, a point facing the camera has zero geometric rim weight. A positive offset lets an environment contribution survive there, still multiplied by the diffuse-plus-ambient lighting factor.

The contrast control raises each cubemap color component to a power. For components between zero and one, a power above one darkens intermediate values. This is an artistic operation, not a new reflection ray.
Two powers operate on the same reflection-light alignment. Their independently colored contributions add together. A smaller exponent gives a broader lobe; a larger exponent gives a tighter one.
Watch the offset increase from zero to one half on the red demo material. Reflection appears more strongly on front-facing regions. The stored environment and the mesh remain the same.
The reflection contribution and both highlights are added to the diffuse base. This makes the controls easy to inspect, but the sum is not an energy-conserving model of layered automotive paint.
Godot's vector power call uses a vector exponent here. The scalar contrast is explicitly expanded into three components. That is a language-porting detail, not an extra physical effect.
Tune each term against a visible goal: reflection at the center, environment contrast, a broad sheen, or a tight highlight. Calling everything shininess hides which calculation you actually changed.

title: The Uber Shader: Reading the Whole
objective: Trace the combined material without assuming earlier texture contracts still apply.
right: every combined input needs its contract checked

terms.Wrap lighting: An artistic broadening of the lit region
terms.Packed map: A texture holding multiple independent controls

exercise: Audit the combined shader's normal-map convention and specular channels. Then vary subsurface spread. Explain the terminator change without describing it as simulated light transport through the material.
checks: Red masks highlights and blue masks reflections.
The green flip matches the supplied DirectX-style map.
recap: The normal-map convention is explicit.
Packed channels differ from the earlier specular map.
Ambient and diffuse use new approximations.
The final color is a sum of identifiable contributions.
beats: This combined shader first decodes its normal map. The green flip defaults to true because the demo supplies the DirectX-style map. Reusing a different normal map requires checking that convention.

Red now masks the highlight, and blue masks the environment reflection. The earlier red-rim, green-highlight packing does not apply. A texture can load successfully while controlling the wrong contribution.

Ambient blends from bottom color toward top color using the upward normal component clamped at zero. Downward and horizontal normals receive bottom color. This is not a symmetric full-sphere interpolation.

Subsurface spread modifies the light-normal dot product before clamping. Subsurface color adds a channel-dependent bias. These are artistic controls that soften and tint the transition around the terminator.

Watch spread increase from zero toward one half. More of the surface receives a positive lighting contribution. No thickness, internal scattering path, or transmitted-light calculation appears in the shader.
The environment contribution has its own contrast, intensity, and blue-channel mask. Unlike the earlier rim-weighted cubemap shader, this reflection is not multiplied by that Fresnel term.

The rim is multiplied by diffuse lighting and light color. The specular lobe uses its red mask. The environment is added separately. Naming each term makes an otherwise crowded expression understandable.

The textured base receives ambient plus direct light, then the extra contributions are added. It is a useful teaching combination, not a complete physical material. Its tangent-frame scaling limitation also remains.
